title: Loop closures and async void
sub: Why the service found zero clashes
cards/0/body:
A building model has hundreds of pipes and beams that cross each other. ClashService starts 8 tasks, and each one checks its own "bucket" of elements. The run finishes without errors and reports: no clashes. But there are clashes.

This is the sneakiest kind of bug: nothing crashed, the answer looks fine, it is just wrong. Let's see where it comes from.
cards/1/title: A lambda holds the box, not the value
cards/1/body:
A lambda does not copy a variable. It remembers the box the variable lives in. In a for loop there is one box i for all iterations. The task from Task.Run peeks into the box only when the thread pool gets to it, and by then the eight-iteration loop has usually finished. The box holds 8.

In foreach every iteration gets a fresh box (since C# 5), so that trap does not exist there.
cards/1/deep: The compiler hoists the captured variable into a hidden closure class (a display class). With for, the variable is declared before the loop body, so there is one instance. With foreach (since C# 5) and with variables declared inside the body, a new instance is created per iteration. The behavior is non-deterministic: a task that managed to start before the next i++ sees a smaller number. That is why the bug "floats" between runs.
cards/2/q: What will ProcessChunk most often receive in the chunk parameter?
cards/2/options/2: Each gets its own number, but in random order
cards/2/explain: By the time the tasks start, the loop has usually finished, and the shared variable is 8. The filter e.Id % 8 == 8 is never true, so no pairs are found at all.
cards/2/wrong/1: That would happen if every lambda saw its own value. But there is one box for all.
cards/2/wrong/2: Random order would need copies. Here the variable is shared, so almost every task sees the final value.
cards/3/task: Here is the launch and the processing of one bucket. Find the bugs: they are about closures, async, lazy enumeration and shared state.
cards/3/bugs/0/why: The caller cannot wait for completion or catch the exception. If ProcessChunk throws, Completed never fires, and the error goes to the SynchronizationContext: in Unity it is just a line in the console, in .NET without a context the process crashes.
cards/3/bugs/1/title: Closure over the loop variable i
cards/3/bugs/1/why: Tasks see the shared i, usually already 8. The chunk filter selects nothing, and the service silently finds zero clashes.
cards/3/bugs/2/why: Elements from different buckets are never compared with each other, so some clashes can never be found. For negative Ids the remainder is negative too.
cards/3/bugs/3/why: mine is a Where recipe, not a list. The inner loop re-runs the filter for every outer element: n² predicate calls, and if the source is lazy too, repeated computation.
cards/3/bugs/4/why: List<T> is not thread-safe. Eight threads corrupt its internal array at the same time: items get lost, exceptions happen.
cards/3/bugs/5/why: The ++ operation is read, add, write. Threads overwrite each other's values, so the count ends up too low. Also, the name _processed promises one thing but counts another.
cards/4/q: Fix the closure: every task needs its own copy of the number.
cards/4/explain: The copy is declared inside the loop body, so each iteration gets a new box. The lambda must use the copy, not i.
cards/5/title: async void: a call with no callback number
cards/5/body:
async Task returns a "receipt": you can wait for completion and learn how it ended. async void gives no receipt. The caller cannot await, and a failure has nobody to catch it.

There is one legitimate use: event handlers (in Unity that includes message methods like async void Start()). Everything else should be async Task.
cards/5/deep: An exception from async void has no Task to live in, so it is rethrown through the SynchronizationContext captured when the method started. In Unity that is UnitySynchronizationContext: the exception runs in its queue on the main thread, Unity logs it to the console, and the game keeps going as if nothing happened. Without a context (a console app, a pool thread) it is thrown on the thread pool as unhandled, and the .NET process terminates. Either way, the code after the failed await never runs: Completed never fires, and whoever waits for it waits forever. Also, a test or the caller cannot await such a method.
cards/6/q: What changes for the caller once RunAsync becomes async Task?
cards/6/options/0: It can await and catch exceptions with try/catch
cards/6/options/2: The method starts running on the main thread
cards/6/explain: A Task gives the caller a point to wait on and a channel for errors. Speed and thread are not affected.
cards/6/wrong/1: Speed is the same. Only what you get back changes.
cards/6/wrong/2: The executing thread is decided by await and the synchronization context, not by the return type.
cards/7/title: Lazy filters and a shared list
cards/7/body:
Where does not filter, it writes down a recipe. Every foreach over it cooks the dish again. Nest one foreach in another and the recipe runs once per outer element.

The second lesson from the kitchen: eight cooks must not write into one notebook at the same time. Either queue up for the notebook (lock), or give each cook their own notebook and glue them together later.
cards/7/code:
var all = elements.ToList();            // once
var mine = all.Where(...).ToList();     // a ready list
var local = new List<Clash>();          // one per task
cards/8/q: Which operations are unsafe when several threads run them on shared fields? Pick all that apply.
cards/8/explain: Add and ++ read and write shared state in several steps. A local variable belongs to its own thread, and Interlocked is atomic.
cards/9/q: Put the steps of a reliable RunAsync in order.
cards/9/items/0: Turn elements into a list once (ToList)
cards/9/items/1: In the loop, make a local copy of the bucket number
cards/9/items/2: Start 8 tasks, each with its own local list
cards/9/items/3: Wait for all of them with await Task.WhenAll
cards/9/explain: First pin down the data and the numbers, then work in parallel with no shared writes, and only after waiting for everyone collect the result on one thread.
cards/10/q: Match each bug with its fix.
cards/10/pairs/0/1: A local copy inside the body
cards/10/pairs/2/0: Lazy Where in a double loop
cards/11/title: For seniors: what else is wrong with the split
cards/11/body: Even after the fixes, the algorithm has a hole. Since pairs are compared only inside a bucket, elements from different buckets never meet. It is better to split the outer loop between tasks (who gets which a) and let the inner loop run over all b. Even better, avoid n² entirely: build a spatial index (a grid, a BVH) and test only neighbors.
cards/11/deep: Note that splitting by Id % 8 can also be uneven (if Ids are issued in steps of 8, say, every element lands in one bucket), and for negative Ids the remainder in C# is negative, so they fall outside 0...7 altogether. For balanced load, prefer Parallel.For with ranges or a Partitioner.
